newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China proposes gutting HK civil liberties laws.
newsitem.headline: China proposes gutting HK civil liberties laws.

text.p: China hit a raw nerve in Hong Kong with proposals to abolish a series of laws on democratic elections and civil liberties when it resumes sovereignty of the British colony this year.

A panel of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee, meeting in Beijing, drew up on Sunday 25 laws and articles, some the product of recent reforms and others the trappings of the colonial era, for repeal or amendment when the British leave at midnight on June 30.
Pro-democracy groups and the colonial government described the move as a blow to democracy and human rights that would dent international confidence in post-1997 Hong Kong.
Governor Chris Patten, architect of recent democratic reforms, lambasted the proposals.
"They strike at the heart of Hong Kong's civil liberties," he said in a statement on Monday.
"They appear to be based on politically motivated pretexts rather than real inconsistencies with the BL (Basic Law)"
The 1990 Basic Law was promulgated by China and serves as Hong Kong's future constitution.
"Some of them (the proposals) appear to be aimed solely at undermining the legal basis for civil liberties in Hong Kong, and they will certainly have that effect," Patten said.
China's Xinhua news agency defended the plans, which it said reversed British reforms that China argues violate the Sino-British treaty governing the handover and the Basic Law.
Both documents promise the 6.3 million people of Hong Kong considerable autonomy in running their affairs and permit the community to retain its freewheeling capitalist way of life.
China has said it will dismantle the Patten reforms, which expanded democracy in Hong Kong.
It has already appointed a provisional legislature to supplant the elected Legislative Council on July 1.

The new lawmaking body will hold its first formal session on Saturday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen across the border from Hong Kong, and is expected to begin work on repealing and re-drafting the 25 laws and articles.
Many in Hong Kong fear the interim chamber will roll back the freedoms Hong Kong has enjoyed, particularly in the twilight of British rule, by implementing draconian new laws.

"Obviously this tells people that evil laws to impede human rights will be restored," said Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's largest party, the Democratic Party, which has boycotted the provisional legislature.
"It's not yet July 1 and (they) have already done many things that make Hong Kong people and foreign governments doubt whether Hong Kong's human rights will be protected in future."
The Legislative Council has called a special session on Friday to discuss the Chinese plans. Representatives from Hong Kong's Bar Association and the Law Society have been invited.

Among the laws to be diluted are Hong Kong's Bill of Rights, a 1992 election law, the Societies Ordinance which permits the formation of political parties and a 1995 Public Order Ordinance which allows peaceful demonstrations.
The changes echo proposals made two years ago by one of the early China-controlled panels, now defunct, the Preparatory Working Committee.
China replaced it with the 150-member Preparatory Committee of mainland officials and pro-Beijing advisers from Hong Kong set up last year to shape Hong Kong's transition.
The Committee selected the caucus that appointed shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa as the territory's post-colonial leader and the 60 members of the provisional legislature.
